pulls.title: i2p: pass base32 address directly to stream connect
pulls.body:
As the SAM protocol accepts a `.b32.i2p` address as the `DESTINATION` parameter for the `STREAM CONNECT` command, the `NAMING LOOKUP` round trip can be skipped on every outbound connection.

This should ostensibly make failure handling more accurate in certain situations as well, since a peer that cannot be resolved now returns `CANT_REACH_PEER`/`TIMEOUT` rather than there being an empty `VALUE=` key in the lookup reply. A missing `VALUE=` is a proxy error, so the attempt isn't recorded in AddrMan.

Router implementation versions that support this (Java I2P 0.9.48, i2pd 2.38.0) are older than ones supporting `i2cp.leaseSetEncType=6,4` (see #35696), so there should be no compatibility issues here.

Source:
https://i2p.net/en/docs/api/samv3/#sam-virtual-streams-connect

pulls.title: kernel: Dispatch log callbacks with btcsignals
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A kernel application whose log callback logs, or destroys a kernel object, hangs. The common way to hit this is a garbage-collected language binding: Python's garbage collector can run finalizers inside the callback, and a finalizer that destroys a chainstate manager flushes and logs (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34775#issuecomment-6278257737, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34374#discussion_r4030551866). The cause is that the kernel calls log callbacks while holding the logger's mutex, so any logging from inside a callback blocks on a mutex its own thread already holds. The problem is not new and has existed since logging callbacks were introduced in #30595.

**Solution:** This PR delivers log entries through `btcsignals::signal`, which calls callbacks without holding any lock, replacing the kernel's own callback list and custom dispatching mechanism.

The change is a usability improvement and a bugfix because with it applications no longer need to reason about deadlocks and blocking behavior from a mutex they can't see. However, they may need to be updated to deal with log callbacks that are no longer serialized and connection functions that no longer block. Compatibility details are in the commit message.

The main code change is in `src/kernel/bitcoinkernel.cpp` (+42/-77) accompanied by header docs and new test_kernel cases, which hang without the fix. There is also a commit switching `btcsignals.h` to use `StdMutex` instead of `Mutex` so it is safe to use in logging callbacks.

This is an alternative to the last commit of #34775, which fixes the same deadlock but only after limiting the process to one logging connection, and still hangs if a callback destroys the connection.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: replace `loadtxoutset` RPC with a startup arg
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Loading a UTXO snapshot through RPC requires coordinating with the active chain, mempool, caches and advertised services while the node is running.

**Fix:** Replace the `loadtxoutset` RPC with `-loadtxoutset=<file>` and finish importing during chainstate initialization, before networking and mempool loading begin.
Require a receiver that has not advanced beyond genesis, already knows the snapshot base header and has no stored blocks beyond genesis or unfinished reindexing.
This removes runtime activation checks, temporary import cache resizing and service demotion while preserving snapshot validation, resumption and background validation.

pulls.title: cmpctblock: Cache serialized cmpctblock msg for relay [part of prefill series]
pulls.body:
This PR extends the optimization added in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/23880 which applies to peers that have requested HB blocks from us to also cache the serialized blocks for low-bandwidth peers. The core change here comes from the closed #26755 made by andrewtoth, but also includes other refactors and type safety improvements.

Performance is less critical for low-bandwidth peers, so this change on its own should have little impact on block propagation, but these refactors are useful as part of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35558 which adds prefilling of compact blocks, and where we run the risk of potentially having to serialize more than one cmpctblock_msg (one prefilled and one not-prefilled).

pulls.title: p2p: ignore historical blocks when counting blocks in flight
pulls.body:
While background validation runs after loading an assumeutxo
snapshot, blocks needed only by the background (historical) chainstate
are also tracked in mapBlocksInFlight. The condition that decides
whether a new block is requested as a compact block counted those
blocks as well, so with historical blocks in flight the new block at
the tip was requested as a full block instead.

Do not count blocks that are only needed by the historical chainstate.
Compact block relay then works normally during background validation.

Behavior is unchanged when no snapshot is loaded, because in that case
there are no historical blocks to exclude.

pulls.title: wallet, sqlite: Enable secure_delete by default
pulls.body:
Currently, when we make deletions or updates to the database that require records to be fully deleted and to not persist in free pages afterwards, we need to explicitly call `WalletDatabase::Rewrite`. This behavior was introduced in #635 to ensure that unencrypted private keys are erased from the database after encrypting a wallet, and initial encryption is the only consumer of this function.

However, initial encryption is not the only functionality that requires secure deletion. l0rinc's LLMs recently found changing the passphrase can leave the original that encryption key record in free pages. We should want to ensure that those records are also deleted, although I do not consider that the presence of such records in free space to actually be a problem. Note that this behavior appears to be present since wallet encryption was initially introduced in #352.

Fortunately, SQLite offers a secure_delete flag that can be enabled on each connection to a database. If set, all deletes or updates will ensure that any data that was deleted or overwritten actually are overwritten with 0's. It is one of the 2 methods in SQLite's documentation for ensuring that records do not persist in free pages, the other method being to call `VACUUM` after deletions or updates, which is what `Rewrite` does.

The downside is that secure_delete will increase CPU and disk I/O, which is why this was not set previously. However, it seems like several distros ship with secure_delete enabled by default: [Debian](https://sources.debian.org/src/sqlite3/3.54.1-2/debian/rules#L48#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), [Ubuntu](https://git.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/sqlite3/plain/debian/rules#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), [Fedora](https://src.fedoraproject.org/rpms/sqlite/raw/rawhide/f/sqlite.spec#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE=1), [Arch](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/archlinux/packaging/packages/sqlite/-/raw/main/PKGBUILD#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), and [NixOS](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/pkgs/development/libraries/sqlite/default.nix#L184) all set SQLite's compile time option to default secure_delete to enabled, and these are just the ones I've looked at. This suggests to me that the performance penalty is not actually that bad. As I run Arch and often do not use depends builds, I had not noticed that secure_delete was always on and did not experience any particularly poor wallet performance that could be attributed to that behavior. In the grand scheme of things, erases and updates are fairly infrequent in the wallet.

This PR enables secure_delete when the database is opened, and also enables it by default in the sqlite depends package. There are also a couple tests to check that all records we want deleted actually are being deleted from the database. `WalletDatabase::Rewrite` is removed as it it is no longer used.

pulls.title: torcontrol: send -torpassword hex-encoded to avoid escaping bugs
pulls.body:
The Tor password was sent as a `QuotedString` with only double quotes escaped; as Tor interprets backslash escapes inside it, any password containing a backslash was mangled (or left the string unterminated).

The Tor Control spec deliberately allows the token to be sent as unquoted hex "to avoid escaping issues", as the `SAFECOOKIE` response already is. This patch does the same for the password, and also adds a functional test covering backslashes and quotes.

pulls.title: net: option to disallow v1 connection on ipv4 and ipv6 peers
pulls.body:
resolves #29618.

This PR adds a config flag option `-v2onlyclearnet` which disallows outbound v1 connections on ipv4 and ipv6 networks since they're unencrypted. outbound v1 connections are still possible from tor/i2p/cjdns peers since they're encrypted networks.

- v1 outbound connections to peers are not attempted
- v1 reconnections are not attempted (if peer is falsely advertised as v2 peer and we attempt a v2 connection but it fails, we do not attempt a v1 reconnection when `-v2onlyclearnet` is switched on)

Currently 70% of reachable nodes in network supporting v2 (according to https://21.ninja/reachable-nodes/node-service-share/ and https://bitnodes.io/nodes). Also found 81% of addresses supporting v2 in the addrman of nodes I checked - personal node and the nodes in [peer.observer](https://peer.observer/addrman/alice). (You can use [this branch ](https://github.com/stratospher/bitcoin/commits/addrinfo_service_display/)to check the % of v2 addresses in a node's addrman.)

EDIT: see [summary](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30951#issuecomment-4346061700) on pros and cons for whether to allow v2 inbounds or not for `-v2onlyclearnet`.

pulls.title: fuzz: torcontrol: drive the control connection over a mocked socket
pulls.body:
The `torcontrol` fuzz target hands made-up replies straight to the `TorController` callbacks, and caps reply lines at 16 characters. As a result, most success paths can't be reached, and the code that parses the control port (`ProcessBuffer()`, `ReceiveAndProcess()`) never runs.

This rewrites the target around a fake Tor on the other end of a real `TorControlConnection`, connected through `DynSock`. Replies go over the wire. The fake Tor answers each command the controller sends with a reply of the matching shape, so inputs can complete the whole handshake: PROTOCOLINFO, authentication (including SAFECOOKIE), GETINFO and ADD_ONION. The harness also checks that reply data never splits a command or injects a new one.

The first commit fixes `DynSock::Wait()`, which deleted its own socket. The bug has been there since #30205; this target is the first caller.

### Testing

Line coverage of `src/torcontrol.cpp` goes from 52% on master to 81% after a 10-minute local run. The master number is from the qa-assets corpus. Most of what remains is the controller thread itself, which the harness replaces, and socket errors that `DynSock` can't produce.

The input format changes, so the corpus in qa-assets needs a refresh.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Skip legacy wallet records rather than erasing them, and drop unused record erase functions
pulls.body: When migrating a legacy wallet, we can skip the records in `MigrateToSQLite` that we would delete later on during migration. These records are specifically all of the legacy wallet records, and transaction records. The legacy wallet records are replaced with descriptor records produced during migration, and transaction records are already being rewritten by migration, so not writing them in the first place is also fine. This allows us to remove several database record erase functions, specifically EraseTx and EraseRecords.

pulls.title: test: Cover 64-bit flatfile position boundaries
pulls.body:
This adds regression tests for the 64-bit file positions introduced by [bitcoin/bitcoin#36669](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36669). Existing flatfile tests use small offsets. The VARINT overflow tests added in [bitcoin/bitcoin#36725](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36725) don't check that `FlatFilePos` preserves a 64-bit position or that opening a file uses the full offset.

The tests check serialization around 2 GiB and 4 GiB, plus zero and `UINT64_MAX`. They also check opening and seeking around 2 GiB and 4 GiB, including preservation of the position across `size()`. The file stays one byte so no data is written at a large offset.

Validation process:

- On macOS arm64 (Apple Clang 21), Linux x86_64/i386 (GCC 13), and Windows x86_64 (clang-cl 22), `flatfile_tests`, `serialize_tests`, `streams_tests`, and `blockmanager_tests` pass. Include/test linters, changed-range clang-format, and whitespace checks also pass locally.
- Before #36669, the existing flatfile tests pass, while the new tests catch rejected serialization and a seek position wrapping to zero at 4 GiB.
- Casting only the current `FlatFileSeq::Open` seek offset to `uint32_t` also makes the new positioning test fail while existing flatfile tests pass on macOS, Linux x86_64, and Windows x86_64.

On non-Windows systems with 32-bit `long`, the seek test warns and returns because the current wrapper uses `fseek`. The serialization test still runs. This behavior was verified on Linux i386. These were focused checks; the full CI matrix has not run.

CI results: [Linux x86_64](https://github.com/john-lawniczak/bitcoin/actions/runs/43471513629/job/132044496559), [Windows x86_64](https://github.com/john-lawniczak/bitcoin/actions/runs/43471513629/job/132044497097), [Linux i386](https://github.com/john-lawniczak/bitcoin/actions/runs/43472008804/job/132046036624). All jobs tested commit `1d11bd83d892d5bdac759e98321899d60f7c84e8`.

pulls.title: wallet: fix migration with watch-only transactions
pulls.body:
Fixes #36483

As described in the linked issue, migration to descriptor wallets currently fails for legacy wallets that contain no spendable keys and are tracking watch-only transactions.

When a database transaction containing `RemoveTxs()` is aborted, the database rolls back and the registered `on_abort` callback is invoked. The current listener contains an empty `std::function` so calling it throws `std::bad_function_call` and masks the actual migration error.

The first commit changes the callback to a no-op function since no memory cleanup happens on abort. It also adds a unit test to confirm that abort restores the database record and leaves wallet memory unchanged.

After this commit, the [functional test](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36483) supplied by the issue's author reports `Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)`, exposing the migration error previously masked by the abort callback exception.

During wallet migration, `RemoveTxs()` defers deletion of transactions from the original wallet's in-memory `mapWallet` until after the database commit. The current check that requires an empty map before the database commit causes migration  to fail.

The second commit checks that the transaction IDs left in the map exactly match those already scheduled to be removed in the `txids_to_delete` vector. If they match, migration continues and the `on_commit` callback removes those transactions from memory.

A new functional test is added to cover migration of a blank wallet with watch-only transactions. It checks that the destination watch-only wallet retains both transactions and balance, including after unloading and reloading the wallet, without rescanning the blockchain.

pulls.title: rpc: Return the right RPCErrorCode more consistently
pulls.body:
Currently, rpc code may return the wrong `RPCErrorCode`. This is perfectly fine, because they should be hit rarely in production.

However, it could be good to be self-consistent. (Otherwise, we could just remove the different error codes and return a single one)

So fix a few error codes:

* An integral out-of-range is now `RPC_TYPE_ERROR`, not `RPC_MISC_ERROR`
* Some invalid args are now `RPC_INVALID_PARAMETER`
* Some transient issues or user-config issues are now `RPC_MISC_ERROR`

pulls.title: build: explicitly disable cl.exe
pulls.body:
Since 4f1e6de6 (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31507), cmake for visual studio can only generate projects that use clang-cl.
But calling cmake without '--preset windows' or '-T ClangCL' still silently generates projects that cannot build anymore.

For example, a build with cl now fails in minisketchwrapper.c because we don't pass anymore a cl option to set __cplusplus value properly.

I propose we explicitly tell at cmake time that this can't work anymore. If not, a lot of windows devs who use cmake without presets will lose time on this.

pulls.title: descriptor: compare x-only public keys in Tapscript Miniscript duplicate check
pulls.body:
In Tapscript Miniscript descriptors (`tr()`), public keys serialize as 32-byte x-only pubkeys per BIP-340, BIP-342, and BIP-379, discarding parity. However, `KeyParser::KeyCompare` in `src/script/descriptor.cpp` compared keys as full 33-byte `CPubKey`s, retaining the parity byte.

When a descriptor contains public keys that differ only in parity prefix (such as `pk(X)` alongside `pk(03X)` where `X` defaults to `02`, or `pk(02X)` alongside `pk(03X)`), `KeyParser::KeyCompare` treated them as distinct keys. Miniscript duplicate key checking passed, declaring the descriptor sane even though both branches serialize on-chain to `<X> OP_CHECKSIG`. Because a single signature satisfies both branches, third parties could malleate transactions by altering branch selectors without holding private keys, violating BIP-379 non-malleability invariants.

This patch updates `KeyParser::KeyCompare` in `src/script/descriptor.cpp` and `KeyConverter::KeyCompare` in `src/test/miniscript_tests.cpp` to compare keys as `XOnlyPubKey` whenever `miniscript::IsTapscript(m_script_ctx)` evaluates true. Under Tapscript context, keys sharing identical x-coordinates compare equivalent (`!comp(a, b) && !comp(b, a)`), ensuring `DuplicateKeyCheck()` detects the collision and rejects the descriptor. In `src/test/descriptor_tests.cpp`, unit tests verify that `tr()` descriptors containing parity-differing duplicate keys (including public hex and private WIF formats) are rejected as not sane, while `wsh()` descriptors continue to treat 33-byte compressed keys with differing parities as distinct.

Fixes #36414.

pulls.body:
The kernel creates its block storage inside `btck_chainstate_manager_create`, configures it through the chainstate manager's options and reads blocks through the chainstate manager. Pruning (#35627) needs block storage that the caller can configure, keep and prune directly.

This adds `btck_BlockManagerOptions` and `btck_BlockManager`. `btck_chainstate_manager_create` takes a block manager and keeps a shared reference to it, so either handle can be destroyed first. A block manager can be passed to only one chainstate manager, and a failed creation still uses it up unless the contexts differ. `btck_block_read` and `btck_block_spent_outputs_read` take the block manager, and block tree entries are valid for its lifetime, which can be longer than the chainstate manager's.

Changes for callers:
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_create` no longer takes a blocks directory.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_set_wipe_dbs` is replaced by `btck_block_manager_options_update_wipe_block_tree_db` and `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_wipe_chainstate_db`. The block tree db is wiped when the block manager is created, and wiping it also wipes the chainstate db, which the old function required anyway.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_block_tree_db_in_memory` moves to the block manager options.
- Both options objects take the same total database cache, and each uses its own share.

pulls.title: kernel: add manual pruning
pulls.body:
Part of #35627 and kernel-node/kernel-node#111. The kernel can't open a data directory that a pruned node created, and it has no way to prune.

This adds a prune option on the block manager, `btck_block_manager_prune_up_to_height` and `btck_chainstate_manager_flush`. With the option set, the kernel opens pruned data directories. The chainstate manager created with the block manager decides what may be deleted, so pruning fails without one.

Pruning writes only block storage, never the chainstate. After an unclean shutdown the chainstate on disk is at the last flush, and recovering from there needs the blocks above it. Pruning therefore keeps every block above the fork point between the last flushed block and the active chain, and reports `btck_PruneStatus_NEEDS_FLUSH` when that bound limited what it could delete. The caller can flush and prune again.

The fork point matters when the flushed block was reorged out. Recovery then disconnects the stale blocks, which needs their block and undo data, and connects the new ones from their block data. `btck_block_manager_prune_reorg_tests` covers that case and fails if the bound uses the flushed block's height instead.

A fast prune option lets tests prune, since test chains never fill a 128 MiB block file.

Based on #36738 and #36854. Draft until both are merged.

pulls.title: rpc: fail scanblocks when block filter range is unavailable
pulls.body:
### The issue

`scanblocks` reads block filters over a range via `LookupFilterRange`. When the
block filter index is behind the active chain (e.g. right after startup, while
it is still syncing in the background), the lookup for the not yet indexed range
fails. The old code ignored that failure, advanced `start_index` to the end of
the chunk, and kept going - so the scan skipped every unindexed block and still
returned `"completed": true`.

The result is a silent gap: a caller gets a `relevant_blocks` list that looks
fine but is missing any match in the unindexed range, with no way to
distinguish "no matches" from "range was never scanned".

Note that `"completed"` only means the scan was not aborted - it does not mean
every filter in the requested range was actually read.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a node with `-blockfilterindex=1` and let it mine/receive some blocks.
2. Stop the node, delete `<datadir>/<chain>/indexes/blockfilter`, restart with
   `-blockfilterindex=1`.
3. Immediately (before the index finishes rebuilding) call
   `scanblocks start '["addr(<addr>)"]'`.

Before this change the call returns `"completed": true` with an empty/partial
`relevant_blocks`, silently skipping the range the index had not rebuilt yet.

### How it is fixed and why

Mirror `getblockfilter`'s error classification:

- Call `BlockUntilSyncedToCurrentChain()` only to obtain an `index_ready` flag.
  Do **not** fail unconditionally when the index is still behind the tip - the
  requested range may already be available.
- If `LookupFilterRange` fails and the index is not ready, throw the same
  "still in the process of being indexed" `RPC_MISC_ERROR` that
  `getblockfilter` uses.
- If `LookupFilterRange` fails after the index is ready, throw
  `RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR` (unexpected / corruption), instead of skipping the chunk.

This closes the silent gap without rejecting scans whose range is already
covered while the index catches up to the tip.

The diff also reindents the match loop: inverting `if (LookupFilterRange(...))`
into an early `throw` removes one nesting level from the existing body. That
reindentation is a consequence of the bug fix, not a standalone style change.

### Tests

- `test/functional/rpc_scanblocks.py` - new `test_scanblocks_unindexed_range`
  covers the modified code: it pads the chain, wipes the filter index, restarts,
  and while the index is behind the tip asserts that a scan to the tip returns
  the indexing error, that a scan over an already-written prefix (genesis)
  still succeeds, and that after sync the match is found.
- The existing `run_test` cases (which `wait_until(... synced ...)` before
  scanning) continue to exercise the normal synced path.

### AI / tooling note

I found this regression while reviewing the RPC with an AI-assisted tool.
I reproduced the unsynced-index behavior myself, chose to mirror
`getblockfilter`'s existing guard, and verified the fix with the
functional test above. This PR text and any review replies are my own.

pulls.title: net: defer compact filter requests that race the filter index
pulls.body:
This PR is another approach to fix a race condition bug when a yet-unconstructed compact filter is requested for an already known block.

Fixes: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/29655, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/27085
Related discussion: [1](https://bnoc.xyz/t/request-block-filter-peers-being-disconnected-due-to-invalid-block-requests/101/2), [2](https://github.com/lightninglabs/neutrino/issues/338)
Another approach which received NACK: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35262

**The problem:**
Bitcoin Core receives a new block and processes it, then advertises it; however, by that moment the compact filter might not yet have been constructed. If a peer asks for a filter in that time window, Bitcoin Core simply does not respond. From the peer's perspective this is a misbehaviour (we advertised a block and don't provide filters for it), which results in disconnects or bans. While it does not critically affect core nodes, it breaks the network topology for BIP 157 clients.

More precisely, [BIP157](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0157.mediawiki#getcfilters) specifies that for `getcfilters` requestor:

```
StopHash MUST be known to belong to a block accepted by the receiving peer. This is the case if the peer had previously sent a headers or inv message with that block or any descendents. A node that receives getcfilters with an unknown StopHash SHOULD NOT respond.
```

Current behaviour clearly contradicts the above specification.

**Proposed solution:**

A `getcfilters`, `getcfheaders` or `getcfcheckpt` request that is racing the filter index is parked instead of being ignored:

  1. `PeerManagerImpl::ShouldDeferCFilterRequest` checks whether a request is racing the index construction: the index is synced, but has not yet caught up with the tip, and does not cover the requested stop hash yet. It never defers during IBD, where the index can lag the tip for a long time.
  2. If so, the request is stored in the peer's `m_pending_request` and we stop processing further messages from that peer. This keeps responses in order; other peers and outgoing messages are not affected.
  3. The parked request is retried whenever we process that peer's messages, at most once every 100ms (`PARKED_CF_RETRY_INTERVAL`) to avoid taking `cs_main` too often.
  4. If the request is still parked after 5s (`MAX_CF_PARK_INTERVAL`), we stop waiting and serve what we can: the peer gets the answer if the filters exist by then, otherwise the request is ignored, as it was before this PR. The peer then continues to be processed normally.


 **Tests:**

A new `cfilter_race_tests` suite (`src/test/cfilter_race_tests.cpp`) uses a `PreFilterBlocker` `CValidationInterface` registered before the filter index, so its own `BlockConnected` fires first on the scheduler thread and stalls it before the filter index gets to run `CustomAppend`. This reproduces the race window deterministically. The tests drive the real message processing path via `ConnmanTestMsg` and advance the mocked clock where time matters.

Cases covered:

  - `deferred_cfilter_response_reaches_peer` — a racing `getcfilters` is parked, not answered and not dropped, and is answered once the index catches up.
  - `deferred_cfheaders_response_reaches_peer` — the same for `getcfheaders`.
  - `pending_request_pauses_message_processing` — while a request is parked, a later `ping` from the same peer is not processed, and the responses come back in request order.
  - `parked_request_retries_are_throttled` — a parked request is not retried before the retry interval has passed, even if the filter is ready.
  - `parked_request_is_released_after_timeout` — after the park timeout the peer is no longer paused (a later `ping` is answered), and no filter is sent for a filter that does not exist.

  I've used Claude Code for this PR.

pulls.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pulls.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

pulls.title: refactor: break the blockstorage/validation circular dependency
pulls.body:
`node/blockstorage.cpp` includes `validation.h`, and the lint lists `node/blockstorage -> validation -> node/blockstorage` as an expected circular dependency. This removes it, and the lint confirms the cycle is gone.

The largest user of validation in block storage is `ImportBlocks`, which drives validation. It moves to `node/chainstate` and sets the reindex flag through the new `BlockManager::SetBlockfilesIndexed()`, which writes the flag to the block tree database and sets the in-memory flag under one `cs_main` hold. The last commit moves `FatalError` to `kernel/fatal_error.h`, after which `blockstorage.cpp` no longer includes `validation.h`. `validation.h` still exports `FatalError` for its other users.

Validation also reaches into `BlockManager`'s private members as a friend. `RequestPrune()` and `MarkBlockIndexDirty()` replace the friend declarations, keeping `m_check_for_pruning` and `m_dirty_blockindex` non-public. Both require `cs_main`, and the annotations let the compiler check it. After this, nothing outside `BlockManager` writes its private state or the block tree database.

There is no behavior change to my knowledge.

Based on #36738. Draft until it is merged.

Thanks to musaHaruna, who [suggested `RequestPrune()`](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#discussion_r4283138022) in his review on my fork. The flag marks a pending pruning check, so callers request it and storage decides whether anything qualifies, which keeps the flag private once the friend declarations are gone.

pulls.title: Configuration argument handling improvements.
pulls.body:
Several numeric configuration options now reject values that are out of range instead of silently wrapping or inverting. Previously a negative value could disable the intended limit entirely.

  - `-dbbatchsize` and `-dbcrashratio` must be non-negative. A negative `-dbbatchsize` wrapped to a huge value and disabled batch flushing, so a reindex could hold an unbounded batch in memory.
  - `-limitclustersize`, `-limitancestorcount`, `-limitdescendantcount`, `-mempoolexpiry`, `-datacarriersize`, `-maxsendbuffer`, `-maxreceivebuffer`, `-bantime`, `-bytespersigop` and `-maxtipage` must be non-negative.

  `-limitclustersize=0`, `-datacarriersize=0`, `-mempoolexpiry=0`,
  `-maxtipage=0`, `-bytespersigop=0`, `-maxsendbuffer=0`,
  `-maxreceivebuffer=0` and `-bantime=0`.

- The `-help` output for `-bytespersigop`, `-datacarriersize`, `-dbbatchsize`, `-stopatheight` and `-checkblockindex` now shows the `=<n>` placeholder for their value, matching how they are actually parsed.

pulls.title: wallet: Clear streams before advancing BDB cursor
pulls.body:
This fixes a case where migratewallet can reject an old wallet as corrupt. The v2 key metadata may include an extra flag byte that Core’s metadata loader leaves unread.

LoadRecords reuses its key and value streams between records. BerkeleyROCursor::Next() appends to those streams, so unread bytes from one record become part of the next and can cause a deserialization error.

Clear both streams before copying the next record, matching SQLiteCursor::Next(). This keeps the existing metadata parsing and migration code.

The regression test reads two records while leaving part of the first key and value unread, then checks that the second record replaces both outputs.

Testing on Linux:
- Without the fix, the regression fails both stream-content checks.
- With the fix, test_bitcoin --run_test=db_tests passes all tests

pulls.title: rpc: Manual prune lock management (Take 2)
pulls.body:
This is a refreshed version of #19463, which was closed due to inactivity.

Motivation: On pruned nodes, if a wallet is not loaded while the node is running, blocks necessary for rescanning when the wallet is loaded may be pruned. This PR allows users and external wallet software to manually manage prune locks via RPC, so they can protect blocks needed for future rescans and also clean up locks that are no longer relevant (e.g. after permanently unloading a wallet from a node). This is useful both for Bitcoin Core's own wallet and for external wallets that use Bitcoin Core as a backend. Usage of temporary prune locking may also be helpful in other functional test scenarios but I didn't spend time to check where might apply.

This PR leverages the existing prune locks system we already have. The interface of the RPCs of the old PR has been slightly updated, it now matches the pattern used by `setban`/`listbanned` exactly. The locks are prefixed to distinguish them from the systems locks and prevent naming colissions. They are not persisted across restarts.

pulls.title: refactor: Add util::Result failure types and ability to merge result values
pulls.body:
Add `util::Result` support for returning more error information and make use of it in [LoadChainstate method](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25665/commits/b1c0feb6656befc48a6840c1d841074bd6131b78) as an initial application. Followup PRs [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) and [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) use it more broadly to return errors and warnings from wallet and kernel functions as well.

This change adds two major features to the result class:

- For better error handling, adds the ability to return a value on failure, not just a value on success. This is a key missing feature that makes the result class not useful for functions like `LoadChainstate()` which produce different errors that need to be handled differently [^1].

[^1]: Ability to return error values was actually present in the original implementation of [#25218](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25218), but unfortunately removed in later iterations. See [design notes](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/bitcoin-devwiki/wiki/util::Result-design-notes).

- For better error reporting, adds the ability to return warning messages and multiple errors, not just a single error string. This provides a way for functions to report errors and warnings in a standard way, and simplifies interfaces:

    ```diff
    -virtual std::unique_ptr<Wallet> loadWallet(const std::string& name, bilingual_str& error, std::vector<bilingual_str>& warnings) = 0;
    +virtual util::Result<std::unique_ptr<Wallet>> loadWallet(const std::string& name) = 0;
    ```

    ```diff
    -std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options, DatabaseStatus& status, bilingual_str& error);
    +util::Result<std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase>, DatabaseError> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options);
   ```

This change also makes some more minor improvements:

- Smaller type size. `util::Result<int>` is 16 bytes, and `util::Result<void>` is 8 bytes. Previously both were 72 bytes.

- Broader type compatibility. Supports noncopyable and nonmovable success and error types.

### Comparison with `std::expected`

Currently, the `util::Result` class is useful for error reporting—returning translated, user-facing error strings—but not as useful for error handling, where callers need structured failure information to decide how to proceed. By contrast, `std::expected` / `util::Expected` (#34005, #34006) is good for error handling but less helpful for reporting. This PR closes the gap between the two classes.

With this PR, `std::expected` remains a good choice for lower-level functions or simple functions that fail in only a few well-defined ways. Meanwhile,

- `Result` becomes a better choice for operations that can fail in many different ways—loading a wallet, connecting a block, etc.—where callers may want complete error traces, not just low-level errors without context or high-level errors without detail. (Followup [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) applies this to wallet-loading functions.) 
- `Result` can also be more useful than `expected` when merging status information from multiple calls. (Followup [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) uses this to reliably propagate flush and fatal-error status from validation code that can internally trigger flushes or shutdowns.)
- `Result` may also be a better choice than `std::expected` when returning pointer values. (Followup [#26022](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022) adds a `ResultPtr` specialization that avoids double dereferencing.) 
- `Result` can be more efficient than `std::expected` when failures are rare but failure objects are large, since failure values are heap-allocated.

This PR effectively makes `Result` a superset of `expected`, making the representations compatible and allowing them to be used together.

pulls.body:
<!-- begin based-on -->
**This is based on #25665.** The non-base commits are:

- [`3d008913cdb` Add util::ResultPtr class](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/3d008913cdb697651e67cd5ee158cc12a9611c0e)
- [`2d0915656c8` Use ResultPtr<unique_ptr> instead of Result<unique_ptr>](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/2d0915656c80d45642965b1963f158d865846f5b)<!-- end -->

---

The `util::ResultPtr` class is a wrapper for `util::Result` providing syntax sugar to make it less awkward to use with returned pointers. Instead of needing to be deferenced twice with `**result` or `(*result)->member`, it only needs to be dereferenced once with `*result` or `result->member`. Also when it is used in a boolean context, instead of evaluating to true when there is no error and the pointer is null, it evaluates to false so it is straightforward to determine whether the result points to something.

This PR is only partial a solution to #26004 because while it makes it easier to check for null pointer values, it does not make it impossible to return a null pointer value inside a successful result. It would be possible to enforce that successful results always contain non-null pointers by using a `not_null` type (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/24423) in combination with `ResultPtr`, though.

pulls.title: wallet: Track no-longer-spendable TXOs separately
pulls.body:
In #27286, the wallet keeps track of all of its transaction outputs, even if they are already spent or are otherwise unspendable. This TXO set is iterated for balance checking and coin selection preparation, which can still be slow for wallets that have had a lot of activity. This PR aims to improve the performance of such wallets by moving UTXOs that are definitely no longer spendable to a different map in the wallet so that far fewer TXOs need to be iterated for the aforementioned functions.

Unspendable TXOs (not to be confused with Unspent TXOs) are those which have a spending transaction that has been confirmed, or are no longer valid due to reorgs. TXOs that are spent in unconfirmed transactions remain in the primary TXO set, and are filtered out of balance and coin selection as before.

pulls.title: http: Restore requirement of IPv4 bind success
pulls.body:
### Problem

When bitcoind starts and the HTTP IPv4 listen address is occupied by another process, but the IPv6 address is available, the server fails open and generates a cookie file. When bitcoin-cli runs it picks up the cookie file and sends the credentials in plain text to the non-bitcoind process running on the default IPv4 port. An attacker can then use the credentials to commandeer bitcoind over IPv6.

### Solution

*Safe defaults*:
* When running with default settings, require that the IPv4 bind succeeds.
* When `-rpcbind` is specified, require that all HTTP listen socket binds succeed (fail closed-behavior).

Node operators who only have IPv6 are now required to override `-rpcbind` and `-rpcallowip` to only specify the working interface and allowed subnet if they were not doing so already.

The problem of bitcoin-cli sending the credentials to what could possibly be the wrong process remains **only in non-default setups**.

### History

40b556d3742a1f65d67e2d4c760d0b13fe8be5b7 from 2015 switched the HTTP server from Boost Asio to LibEvent, and binding switched from an attempt at dual-binding IPv4+v6 and falling back to IPv4-only (rpcserver.cpp / `StartRPCThreads()`), to binding IPv4 *or* IPv6 (httpserver.cpp / `HTTPBindAddresses()`). **The current PR restores the prior behavior of IPv4 being mandatory.**

#14968 from 2018 was an attempt to change the behavior to require *all* binds to succeed. But it ran into issues with poor IPv6 support on CI.

### Severity

This credential exfiltration attack requires capability to launch processes on the bitcoind host. If we are on the same account we can already read the cookie credentials off disk. So it's only really interesting when an attacker is on a different user account on the same host.

pulls.title: rpc: Report -rpcwhitelist denials as JSON-RPC errors
pulls.body:
This PR adds two JSON-RPC error codes for requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist`, which until now got an HTTP 403 status with an empty body:

- `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` (-38) is returned for a refused request, with HTTP 200 for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and 403 for legacy 1.x requests.
- `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` (-39) is returned for the other requests in a refused batch. A refused batch now gets HTTP 200 and an array with an error for each request, and still runs none of them.

**Problem:** `-rpcwhitelist` errors are currently handled differently from other JSON-RPC errors, so clients report them with vague or misleading messages, and for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests the handling does not follow [documented behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md#json-rpc-11-vs-20). Specifically, requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist` get HTTP 403 with an empty body, so the refusal shows up as a generic transport error rather than a specific JSON-RPC error. This is especially a problem for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, which are [supposed to](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/bf1a1f1662427fbf1a43bb951364eface469bdb7) report failed method calls only as JSON-RPC errors, not HTTP errors. The empty reply causes a concrete problem when JSON-RPC requests are sent over IPC instead of HTTP: `bitcoin-cli -ipcconnect` receives only the response body, so a refused call prints a JSON type error instead of a permission error, as described in a [private security review](https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/audits/ar-56/). Over HTTP, `bitcoin-cli` currently stops at the 403 status and prints only "server returned HTTP error 403" instead of the actual error.

**Solution:** Report whitelist denials like any other failed call: a JSON-RPC error in the body, with the HTTP status the request's version calls for. This brings the behavior in line with the documentation. `bitcoin-cli` then prints the permission error over both HTTP and IPC, with no change to the IPC interface. The fix is a small change to `src/httprpc.cpp` and `src/rpc/protocol.h`, with tests in `rpc_whitelist.py` and `interface_ipc_cli.py`. It comes after two refactoring commits suggested in #36642, which move connection fields out of `JSONRPCRequest` into a new `JSONRPCClient` struct and move the batch loop into a `ProcessBatch()` helper that the refused-batch reply shares. Details in the commit messages.

Compatibility: HTTP clients that send `"jsonrpc": "2.0"` or batches and check for a 403 status need to read the error code instead. Single 1.x requests keep the 403 status, now with an error body.

Open question for review: `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` could be named `RPC_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` is documented as batch-specific but would fit any request refused before it runs.

This PR changes the way settings are registered and retrieved to provide more compile-time safety. Currently settings are [registered](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/03cff2c1421e5db59963eba1a845ef5dd318c275/src/init.cpp#L504) and [retrieved](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/03cff2c1421e5db59963eba1a845ef5dd318c275/src/init.cpp#L173) like:

```c++
args.GetPathArg("-pid", BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME)
```

But this is not ideal because nothing checks that setting names are spelled correctly, or that default values (`BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME`) are used consistently in the help string and retrieval sites, or that settings are retrieved with consistent types (bool, int, string, path, or list). This PR addresses these issues by adding setting [declarations](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init_settings.h#L267-L270) which allow settings to be [registered](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init.cpp#L484) and [retrieved](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init.cpp#L164C38-L164C59) like:

```c++
// Declare setting
using PidSetting = common::Setting<
    "-pid=<file>", fs::path, {.legacy = true},
    "Specify pid file. Relative paths will be prefixed by a net-specific datadir location. (default: %s)">
    ::DefaultFn<[] { return BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME; }>;

// Register setting
PidSetting::Register(argsman);

// Retrieve setting
PidSetting::Get(args)
```

---

#### Suggestions for review

All the real changes in this PR are in the last scripted-diff commit:

- [scripted-diff: Replace AddArgs / GetArgs calls with Setting Register / Get calls](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31260/commits/73c1f852eba2a48be0f03816a957e46ce6275bd9)

If you take a few minutes to look at the changes applied in this scripted-diff commit, you'll understand everything this PR is doing. A good place to start looking around in this commit is the generated [`src/init_settings.h`](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/pr/scripty/src/init_settings.h) file which declares the settings that get registered in [src/init.cpp](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/pr/scripty/src/init.cpp). Then you can look at the surrounding diffs and see they are just replacing `AddArg` and `GetArg` calls.

The other notable commit is second commit, which implements the `Setting` class:

- [common: Add Setting class to support typed Settings](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31260/commits/9c1cdb31eac5a180950dee0c6135918ce70b60f1)

The other commits do minor things like moving code or updating linters. The python script that implements the scripted diff is a temporary artifact that gets deleted. The python script is complicated because it does things like parsing c++ code to extract help strings, and figuring out the right types to declare settings with so code compiles. But the entire scope of the script is to (1) generate Setting type definitions, (2) add #includes, and (3) replace `AddArg()` calls with `Register()` calls and `GetArg()` calls with `Get()` calls. So there is not much the script can actually do wrong without triggering build and test failures.

---

#### Extensions

This PR only adds the ability to declare individual settings with built-in types. It doesn't provide any new runtime behavior, but a branch in issue #22978 extends the `Setting` class implemented here to support runtime setting validation, additional types like `std::variant`, additional conversion options, custom types, custom validation, and groups of settings declared as options structs.

This change is mostly orthogonal to #16545. #16545 only provides runtime type checking while this PR only provides compile-time checking with no new runtime behavior. But this change does allow a nicer way of declaring types in #16545, using c++ types like `int` instead of flags like `ALLOW_INT`, or`std::vector<std::string>` instead of `ALLOW_STRING | ALLOW_LIST`.

pulls.title: wallet: allow skipping script paths
pulls.body:
While testing MuSig2 integration in #29675 I ran into a Ledger bug https://github.com/LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin-new/issues/329 that was triggered because we signed for a script path in addition to the key path. The bug itself will be fixed, but it seems useful in general to be able to skip script path signing (and finalizing).

For example, you may have a 2-of-2 musig() descriptor with some sort of fallback after coins are N blocks old. For both on chain privacy and fee reasons, you don't want to use this path unless absolutely necessary. But our wallet can't know if our co-signer still has their key, so we sign the script path at all times. This could lead to accidental broadcast.

This PR introduces a `keypath_only` option (default `false` for now) to the following RPC methods:
- `send` 
- `sendall`
- `walletcreatefundedpsbt`
- `walletprocesspsbt`
- `descriptorprocesspsbt`

The resulting PSBT won't _add_ `taproot_scripts` or `taproot_script_path_sigs`. It does still have `taproot_bip32_derivs` and `musig2_participant_pubkeys`.

It will not remove `taproot_scripts` from an existing PSBT, but it won't add a corresponding entry to `taproot_script_path_sigs`. We also won't finalize a PSBT without keypath spend, even with complete script paths. This protects against other participants accidentally including them.

The `wallet_taproot.py` tests are expanded to cover this behavior.

It can also be tested with https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

pulls.title: wallet: relax external_signer flag constraints
pulls.body:
The `external_signer` indicates that an external signer device may be called via [HWI](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/HWI) or [equivalent](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/external-signer.md#signer-api) application.

When it was initially introduced some additional constraints were placed on wallets with this flag: it had to be a descriptor wallet and watch-only. Also the flag could not be added or removed later.

The constraints aren't a problem for the main supported and documented use case of connecting a single hardware wallet and using it just like a normal single sig Bitcoin Core wallet.

But they get in the way of MuSig2 support, see https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

This pull request drops the following constraints:

- `disable_private_keys` is no longer mandatory (but still default)
- `external_signer` flag is now mutable

Changing the `external_signer` flag reloads the wallet so that its descriptor ScriptPubKeyMans are recreated using the new setting.

Additionally it does the following:

- make the `blank` option for `createwallet` consistent with regular wallets by _not_ importing keys from the connected signer
- avoid going through `createTransaction` for external signers (otherwise the GUI breaks)
- create an `ExternalSignerScriptPubKeyMan` when importing a descriptor into an external signer wallet, instead of requiring an additional reload

This should have no noticeable effect on the default single sig use case described above.

Finally we add test coverage for spending from an imported hot key descriptor in an external signer wallet. The wallet signs with its own keys before involving the external signer.

pulls.title: blocks: add resumable reobfuscation for existing block files
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Nodes that synced before v28 may store block and undo files effectively unobfuscated with a zero XOR key. There is no built-in way to obfuscate those existing files, rotate their key, or deliberately replace it with a zero key without resyncing.

**Fix:** Add `-reobfuscate-blocks[=<value>]` to rewrite existing `blk*.dat` and `rev*.dat` files before chainstate loading. With no value or `=1`, the option generates a random 8-byte key. A 16-character hexadecimal value selects an exact key, including all zeros to remove obfuscation, while malformed values fail during startup. If the selected key is already active, block and undo files are left unchanged.

Files are rewritten in fixed-size chunks, staged with a `.reobfuscated` suffix, committed before the originals are removed, and renamed to their original names after all rewrites finish. The target key is staged as `xor.dat.reobfuscated`, which is also used to resume an interrupted migration. Progress is reported in the log and through kernel notifications marked as resumable.

**Benchmark:** The migration is single-threaded and processes one file at a time.

| CPU | Storage | Block count | Size | Files | Time (min) | Blocks/min |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Apple M4 Max laptop | SSD | ~955k | ~854 GB | 11,232 | 10.18 | 93,804 |
| Intel Core i9 | SSD | ~909k | ~725 GB | 10,238 | 23.1 | 39,351 |
| Raspberry Pi 5 | SSD | ~914k | ~728 GB | 10,276 | 72.78 | 12,558 |
| Intel Core i7 | HDD | ~909k | ~720 GB | 10,156 | 208.7 | 4,356 |
| Raspberry Pi 4B | HDD | ~915k | ~730 GB | 10,304 | 1467 | 624 |

**Similar work:**

- [contrib: add xor-blocks tool to obfuscate blocks directory #32451](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32451)
- [andrewtoth/blocks-xor](https://github.com/andrewtoth/blocks-xor)

pulls.title: mining: add getMemoryLoad() and track template non-mempool memory footprint
pulls.body:
IPC clients can hold block templates indefinitely, keeping transactions alive after they leave the mempool. This adds `getMemoryLoad()` to estimate the memory held on behalf of all mining clients, as discussed in bitcoin/bitcoin#33899. It does not impose a limit.

The estimate includes each tracked template's vectors and the transactions it references that are no longer in the mempool. Transaction objects shared by multiple templates are counted once. Dummy coinbase transactions and the template cached by the `getblocktemplate` RPC are excluded.

`BlockTemplateManager` tracks templates through weak references, so the registry does not prolong their lifetime. Templates unregister when destroyed, including when IPC cleanup happens after shutdown has reset the manager. Clients can reduce the reported memory load by releasing stale templates or explicitly calling `destroy()`.

The result is an estimate: the mempool can change during calculation, and eviction followed by re-entry as a different transaction object can cause undercounting.

Example client usage: [stratum-mining/sv2-tp#63](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-tp/pull/63).

Commits:

- `refactor: pass block template by reference to WaitAndCreateNewBlock`
- `refactor: share ownership of BlockTemplateManager`
- `mining: track block templates held by IPC clients`
- `mining: add GetTemplateMemoryUsage()`
- `ipc: add getMemoryLoad()`
- `test: check template memory accounting invariants`

**Problem:** #34931 made unreadable coin entries fatal, but `CDBWrapper::Read()` still returns `false` for deserialization failures and propagates LevelDB point-read exceptions to callers.
A corrupt txindex point read can consequently fail one RPC while the node continues running.
#35728 reports other txindex lookup failures as errors that callers can also catch while the node continues running.
Chainstate also retains `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher` as a separate view layer to report read errors and abort.

**Fix:** Make LevelDB point-read and typed deserialization failures fatal in `CDBWrapper`, after logging the database path and error and notifying the database owner’s `kernel::Notifications` when supplied.
This includes point-read failures during startup, which now bypass the GUI’s database rebuild offer.
Missing keys still return `false`, database-open failures retain their initialization handling, and iterator behavior remains unchanged.

Pass each owner’s existing notifications at construction for chainstate, the block-index database, optional index databases, and the temporary UTXO database used by `dumptxoutset`.
Remove `TryRead()` and `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher`, keep `HaveCoin()` on the cache view that owns its caching behavior, and mark coin-view lookups `noexcept`.

Make txindex consistency errors and block-file lookup failures fatal through the shared notification path before aborting.
Continue skipping stale entries for unknown blocks and non-active blocks without data.
Direct block reads retain their existing RPC error handling.

pulls.title: wallet: make migration more robust against failures
pulls.body:
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

pulls.title: refactor: Add [[nodiscard]] to functions returning bool+mutable ref
pulls.body:
Legacy code often used a function signature of the form `bool Get...(const& in, mut& in_out);` to implement a getter that optionally returns a value.

In modern code, this can be replaced by `std::optional<_> Get...(const& in);`.

However, some legacy code remains. To ensure that the "imaginary optional" is not unwrapped when the getter returns false, add a C++17 `[[nodiscard]]` attribute to all those legacy functions.

There were only a few places that ignored the return value. I've fixed them in separate commits.

This should be easy to review via `--word-diff-regex=.` and then confirming that the attribute was added to such a getter.

pulls.title: kernel: allow only one global logging connection
pulls.body:
Kernel logging is inherently global: `KernelLogger` is a process-wide
singleton, so every connection receives every log entry and shares the
minimum level. Multiple `btck_LoggingConnection` handles give the false
impression of independent loggers.

Limit `btck_global_logging_connection_create` to a single connection, so
that the globalness is expressed in that one function and the rest of
the interface can operate on the connection handle.

A single connection also makes it straightforward to invoke the callback
without holding the logger's mutex. Holding it serializes all logging
threads on user code, and deadlocks if anything on the callback's thread
logs, e.g. a garbage collector running finalizers that destroy kernel
objects.

Behaviour changes for consumers:
- `btck_logging_connection_create` is renamed to
  `btck_global_logging_connection_create`, and fails if a connection
  already exists.
- `btck_logging_set_min_level` becomes
  `btck_logging_connection_set_min_level`, and each new connection
  starts at `Info`.
- The "Logger connected." `Debug` entry is removed, since it can no
  longer be delivered.
- The callback can be invoked from multiple threads at the same time,
  so it must be thread-safe. Destroying the connection still waits for
  running invocations to return.

pulls.title: validation: improve block data I/O error handling in P2P paths
pulls.body:
Early note: the majority of this PR consists of test coverage. The changes per se are quite small, just the issue shows up in multiple paths in slightly different forms.

The goal of the PR is to ensure I/O errors are not silently ignored during validation or P2P message handling. In some cases, such as `GETDATA` or `GETBLOCKTXN` requests, errors can be swallowed, leaving the node unresponsive to the request without any action. In a harder to reach but more severe case, a swallowed error can leave the node alive but stuck, unable to process new blocks and advance the chain. Also, silently ignoring errors obviously makes problems harder to diagnose. So this PR seeks to improve all of that.

Currently, the same root cause, inability to access the blocks directory, can produce different behaviors depending on where it occurs: 
1. If it happens during block connection, inside `AcceptBlock()`, the error gets caught and triggers a fatal error graceful shutdown. This is the correct behavior.

2. If it happens during block connection (due to the unguarded `FlatFileSeq::Open` -> `fs::create_directories` call), after `AcceptBlock()`, inside `ActivateBestChain()`, the error gets thrown and swallowed by the P2P general try-catch, leaving the node in a living but stuck state. Where `ActivateBestChain()` will always silently fail on any posterior block processing, retrying to active the failing block.

3. If it happens during `GETDATA` request, the file system error gets swallowed by the message handling general try-catch, only logging a net-debug-level message. The remote peer is not disconnected, nor the node aborts. It just silently ignores the request. This is different to a missing block data, which currently logs the error + disconnects the peer.

4. If it happens during `GETBLOCKTXN` request, the file system error either gets swallowed by the message handling general try-catch or crashes the system via an assertion, depending on if the problem is at the blocks directory level or at the block data level, which is inconsistent.

5. If it happens during `GETCFILTERS` request, the file system error gets swallowed by the message handling general try-catch.

6. If this happens in any of the index functions, the node crashes.


So, this PR makes failure handling consistent and ensures the node never enters a stuck state due to a block I/O error. Changes:

1. `GETDATA` now treats the issue in the same way as other I/O errors: it logs the error + disconnect the remote peer.
2. `GETBLOCKTXN` now triggers a fatal error and graceful shutdown. The error here is stricter than in `GETDATA` because it can only access the last 10 blocks, which must be available for reorgs.
3. `ActivateBestChain()` now triggers a fatal error and graceful shutdown when it happens. Fixing the silent stuck node state scenario.
4. `GETCFILTERS` now logs the error through the expected path: "Failed to find block filter in index". A more descriptive error message can be added in a follow-up PR.
5. The index-related functions now ignore the error instead of crashing the node. This matches how the code was written, as these paths were not expecting `OpenFile` to throw. Better error handling can be added in a follow-up PR.


Testing Note
Can reproduce the different behaviors that cause the stuck node scenario by running the second commit’s unit test 28af683b5dfdce88892e367b308857b94ec630fe or by manually introducing an exception in `ConnectTip()` (which occurs inside `ActivateBestChain()`). Previously, the thrown exception would have being caught by the general P2P try-catch and logged only at net-debug level, which most users do not have enabled, leaving the node alive but stuck, as subsequent block connections repeatedly attempt to process the failing block, throw the exception again, and get silently swallowed. Adding a functional test for this scenario is not possible due to the requirement of failing inside `ActivateBestChain()`, which always occurs after `AcceptBlock()`, which correctly captures the error.


Separate Note
There is another assertion scenario that we can move to graceful shutdown (fatal error) in the compact block relay that I haven't done here.

Extra Note
If want to see a similar error producing a crash, but in the wallet, go to #34176.

pulls.title: net: add -outboundbind option for outgoing source address
pulls.body:
Closes #6476

Adds `-outboundbind=<addr>` to set the source address of outgoing clearnet
connections, one per address family. It is separate from `-bind`; without it,
outbound follows the OS routing table as before.

- The command line wins over the config file, as for other options.
- Clearnet only: Tor and I2P use their own transport, CJDNS is direct but not
  IPv4/IPv6, and a proxy leaves the option inert for that family (with a
  startup warning).
- The effective address per family is trial-bound at startup, like `-bind` via
  `BindListenPort`; a port, the wildcard, or a non-clearnet value is rejected. A
  failed bind at connect time aborts the connection, with no fallback.

Functional and unit tests cover both families, the startup rejections, and the
bind-before-connect path.

Based on vasild's approach in
https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/6476#issuecomment-1666472338.

pulls.title: consensus: Remove special treatment for single threaded script checking
pulls.body:
This topic has been motivated by my work on batch validation and a related conversation just happened here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32467#discussion_r2098305199 

`CheckInputScripts` currently only does what its name implies if there is no multithreading usage for validation. If there are worker threads available the function instead only creates the checks and puts them into a vector. Aside from some shared pre-checks the multithreaded code path is much simpler compared to the rest. This dual use makes the function hard to grasp and its naming confusing.

This PR refactors this code to be more readable and improves documentation aside from unifying the single threaded and the multithreaded cases by letting checkqueue handle single threaded script checking as well. The code is already suited for this and there seems to be not noticable performance overhead from this.

pulls.title: refactor: Use CBlockIndex parameters as reference
pulls.body:
This is a janitorial refactor, a continuation of #34440. Input method parameters of type `const CBlockIndex*` are changed to reference `const CBlockIndex&` in some places where it makes no sense to call with a nullptr.

Motivation: slight improvement in code quality, maintainability and robustness.
- more explicit representation of the non-null input invariant
- less chance of nullptr-access error with future code changes
- more explicit checks at call sites for the non-null input invariant.

The following methods are affected:
- `LastCommonAncestor()` in chain.h
- `PeerManagerImpl::FindNextBlocks()` (net_processing.cpp)
- `PeerManagerImpl::TryDownloadingHistoricalBlocks()` (net_processing.cpp)
- `BlockFilterIndex::LookupFilterRange()`, `BlockFilterIndex::LookupFilterHashRange()` (blockfilterindex.h), and `LookupRange()` in blockfilterindex.cpp
- `BaseIndex::ProcessBlock()` (base.h)

General guidelines:
- When a method has an input of type `const CBlockIndex*`, and by contract it cannot be nullptr, change it to `const CBlockIndex&`. The reference type is an implicit documentation of the nun-nullptr invariant.
- When calling a method with reference parameter, ensure that it cannot be nullptr (it is often derived from a pointer), by/because:
  - explicit prior check and error handling
  - an assert/Assert/Assume
  - itself being a non-nullptr invariant input
  - it is being an output from a method with no-nullptr output invariant
- For local variables, use reference types whenever possible, for non-nullptr references
- For technical reasons pointers are still used even in some non-nullptr cases:
  - containers/variables that can staty unitialized initially
  - containers that need `reserve()`
  - using reference type in `std::set` would result in some copy constructor calls
  - `std::optional` cannot hold a reference type

pulls.title: Remove CNode dependency for local address functions and introduce LocalAddressManager
pulls.body:
This is part of the [net/net_processing split](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/33958) project.

This PR _does not_ change any current behavior, though it does highlight some areas for improvement.

### Background

All of this trouble is necessary for a single purpose: advertising our own network address to peers. This currently happens in `PeerManagerImpl::MaybeSendAddr`. 

In order to advertise our network address, we need to know _what_ to advertise. We make our best guess based on these criteria (ordered from worst to best):

```c
enum
{
    LOCAL_NONE,   // unknown
    LOCAL_IF,     // address a local interface listens on
    LOCAL_BIND,   // address explicit bound to
    LOCAL_MAPPED, // address reported by PCP
    LOCAL_MANUAL, // address explicitly specified (-externalip=)

    LOCAL_MAX
};
```

Because we may have more than one publicly visible network address (ipv4, ipv6, tor, etc), we do our best to advertise an address to peers that they would be able to reach. This avoids (for example) disclosing our public ipv4 address to a node connected to our onion service. Accordingly, in order to determine the best address for a given peer which maybe have connected through a proxy, in addition to their address, the LocalAddressManager must also know the network through which they are connected.

We have one last source of data for what our public network address may be: each peer (as part of the version handshake) tells us what they think our address is. This is untrustworthy data, so it is not added to our list of possible addresses for consideration for other peers. We currently only consider advertising it back to a peer (in `GetLocalAddrForPeer`) if it is routable AND either we don't have a good guess OR randomly. The `LocalAddressManager` introduced in this PR is unrelated to that logic.


### What's happening in this PR (and how to review)

- Because local address management is unrelated to `CConnman`, its reliance on them (via `CNode`) is removed.
- `LocalAddressManager` is created in order to house the local network address functionality.
- All functionality is still global in scope, though `LocalAddressManager` is now instantiated when possible for testing and fuzzing
- There should be no behavioral changes

Reviewers should be able to verify that there are no behavioral changes, and that the handling of local address management is now contained and more straightforward.

### Next steps

I stopped at this point because the changes, while straightforward and boring, have already added up. The main obvious change that remains is to remove the `CNode` dependency from `GetLocalAddrForPeer`.

Beyond that:
- Store addrLocal in `Peer` rather than `CNode` as it is an artifact of the message layer, not the networking layer
- Move the `GetLocalAddrForPeer` logic to `PeerMan` for the same reason.
- Instantiate `LocalAddressManager` with options to avoid its use of globals where possible (`fListen`, `fDiscover`, `fLogIPs`).
- Potentially remove `g_localaddressman` and store an instance in `NodeContext` instead.
- From a quick glance, I think that fuzzing is currently broken because `g_reachable_nets` is not populated.

### Potential behavioral improvements

- The (unchanged) logic in `LocalAddressManager::Get` uses a peer's IP and the network through which they're connected to decide which of our addresses to advertise. This address doesn't have much meaning when the peer is connected through an outbound proxy or is inbound via tor.
- Only advertise an address to a peer of the same network through which they're connected to us. OR codify and add tests for what the exceptions should be. The current logic in `LocalAddressManager::Get` and `GetLocalAddrForPeer` is brittle and difficult to reason about.
